6913.title: Open Prompt
6913.heading: Open Prompt
6913.content:
An open prompt invites a wide range of user requests, as in asking how the assistant can help. It gives the user initiative but provides little linguistic constraint to recognition and understanding.

After an open prompt, the system must perform broad [[Intent Triggering]] and [[Candidate Hypothesis Ranking]]. If confidence is low, it can narrow the interaction with a [[Directed Prompt]].

6915.sourceSearchName: open nested transaction open nested transaction
6915.title: Open Nested Transaction
6915.heading: Document

6916.sourceSearchName: open nested transaction open nested transaction
6916.title: Open Nested Transaction
6916.heading: Open Nested Transaction
6916.content:
An open nested transaction can expose its committed effects before the parent transaction finishes. This improves concurrency because other work need not wait for the entire parent.

Early visibility weakens simple rollback: if the parent later aborts, the system may need a compensating action rather than erasing an effect that other transactions have already observed.

6917.sourceSearchName: open nested transaction open nested transaction
6917.title: Open Nested Transaction
6917.heading: References

6918.sourceSearchName: open level layout open level layout
6918.title: Open Level Layout
6918.heading: Document

6919.sourceSearchName: open level layout open level layout
6919.title: Open Level Layout
6919.heading: Open Level Layout
6919.content:
An open level layout gives the player largely unconstrained movement across a broad space. Obstacles and restricted regions may exist, but the player is not forced through one dominant route.

Open layouts support exploration and strategic positioning while making sequence and pacing harder to control. Landmarks, goals, terrain, and information must help players choose direction without requiring a fixed path.

6920.sourceSearchName: open level layout open level layout
6920.title: Open Level Layout
6920.heading: References

6922.title: Open Endpoint
6922.heading: Open Endpoint
6922.content:
An open endpoint is a boundary value excluded from an [[Interval]]. It corresponds to a strict inequality such as (x<2) or (x>-1).

On a [[Number Line]], exclusion is shown with an unfilled circle at the boundary. In interval notation, a parenthesis is used. Values may approach the endpoint arbitrarily closely while the endpoint itself remains outside the set. This differs from a [[Closed Endpoint]], which is included through an equality option.

6925.title: Open Dialog
6925.heading: Open Dialog
6925.content:
Open dialog allows users to express requests without being led through a fixed sequence of narrowly constrained prompts. It supports natural wording and user initiative but creates a much larger interpretation problem.

A broad [[Personal Virtual Assistant]] often begins with an [[Open Prompt]], uses [[Intent Triggering]] to select a domain, and then may shift into more directed task completion.

6927.sourceSearchName: open design principle open design principle
6927.title: Open Design Principle
6927.heading: Document

6928.sourceSearchName: open design principle open design principle
6928.title: Open Design Principle
6928.heading: Open Design Principle
6928.content:
The open design principle says security should not depend on attackers being ignorant of how a system works. Protection should rest on controlled secrets such as keys and on mechanisms that remain sound when the design is public.

Public scrutiny can expose weaknesses and permits independent evaluation. Security through obscurity may add friction, but it cannot substitute for a defensible architecture.

6929.sourceSearchName: open design principle open design principle
6929.title: Open Design Principle
6929.heading: References

6931.title: Ontology
6931.heading: Ontology
6931.content:
An ontology is an explicit organization of concepts, properties, and relationships in a domain. For language understanding, it provides a shared structure into which phrases can be mapped.

An [[Intent Schema]] is a practical, task-oriented form of conceptual organization. Rich ontologies can support inference, but creating and maintaining them is labor-intensive and limits the easy scaling of hand-built understanding systems.

6934.title: OODA Loop
6934.heading: OODA Loop
6934.content:
The OODA loop cycles through Observe, Orient, Decide, and Act. Observation gathers changing evidence, orientation interprets it in context, decision selects a response, and action changes the environment that will be observed next.

For live games, a shorter reliable decision loop lets a team learn and respond faster than a competitor or a slower internal release process.

6936.sourceSearchName: online principal component analysis online principal component analysis
6936.title: Online Principal Component Analysis
6936.heading: Document

6937.sourceSearchName: online principal component analysis online principal component analysis
6937.title: Online Principal Component Analysis
6937.heading: Online Principal Component Analysis
6937.content:
Online principal component analysis updates a low-dimensional linear subspace as new observations arrive. Incremental updates avoid retaining the full data matrix or recomputing an eigendecomposition from scratch.

The method seeks the dominant variance directions available at the current time. Step sizes, numerical stability, changing distributions, and the number of retained components determine how closely the online representation follows a batch solution.

6938.title: Online Principal Component Analysis

6940.title: Online Game
6940.heading: Online Game
6940.content:
An online game is a multiplayer distributed game whose participants' machines communicate over a network. Online describes the connection arrangement rather than a particular genre.

Separate screens allow private information and individual viewpoints, but the design must handle transmission delay, arrival, departure, failure, security, communication, and the social consequences of remote play.

6942.sourceSearchName: online linear discriminant analysis online linear discriminant analysis
6942.title: Online Linear Discriminant Analysis
6942.heading: Document

6943.sourceSearchName: online linear discriminant analysis online linear discriminant analysis
6943.title: Online Linear Discriminant Analysis
6943.heading: Online Linear Discriminant Analysis
6943.content:
Online linear discriminant analysis incrementally updates class-conditioned statistics and a discriminative projection as labeled observations arrive. It aims to preserve separation among classes without storing all earlier examples.

The representation must track both within-class and between-class structure. Small or evolving classes can make covariance estimates unstable, so regularization and adaptive updates are important.

6944.sourceSearchName: online linear discriminant analysis online linear discriminant analysis
6944.title: Online Linear Discriminant Analysis
6944.heading: References

6945.sourceSearchName: online information theoretic metric learning online information theoretic metric learning
6945.title: Online Information-Theoretic Metric Learning
6945.heading: Document

6946.sourceSearchName: online information theoretic metric learning online information theoretic metric learning
6946.title: Online Information-Theoretic Metric Learning
6946.heading: Online Information-Theoretic Metric Learning
6946.content:
Online information-theoretic metric learning updates a Mahalanobis matrix when pairwise constraints arrive sequentially. Each step changes the current metric enough to satisfy the new similarity or dissimilarity bound while limiting information-theoretic divergence from the previous matrix.

The update supports streaming supervision without solving the full batch problem again. Its order-sensitive path makes constraint quality and step control important to stability.

6947.title: Online Information-Theoretic Metric Learning

6949.sourceSearchName: online game player expectations online game player expectations
6949.title: Online Game Player Expectations
6949.heading: Online Game Player Expectations
6949.content:
Online game player expectations are beliefs about what a continuing paid or supported world owes its community. Players may expect fairness, profitable effort, protection before harm, fast problem resolution, and a presumption of honest behavior.

No service can satisfy every expectation. Operators must communicate rules, limits, support commitments, and the consequences of player conduct while recognizing that taking payment creates an ongoing obligation.

6950.sourceSearchName: online game player expectations online game player expectations
6950.title: Online Game Player Expectations

6951.sourceSearchName: ongoing responsibility register ongoing responsibility register
6951.title: Ongoing Responsibility Register
6951.heading: Document

6952.sourceSearchName: ongoing responsibility register ongoing responsibility register
6952.title: Ongoing Responsibility Register
6952.heading: Ongoing Responsibility Register
6952.content:
An ongoing responsibility register identifies work that must recur throughout development rather than finish once, such as maintaining builds, updating documentation, organizing tests, or checking asset integration. It names an owner without reducing the responsibility to a single checkbox.

Separating recurring duties from ordinary tasks prevents essential maintenance from disappearing each time the immediate task list is reprioritized.

6954.sourceSearchName: online correlation clustering online correlation clustering
6954.title: Online Correlation Clustering
6954.heading: Document

6955.sourceSearchName: online correlation clustering online correlation clustering
6955.title: Online Correlation Clustering
6955.heading: Online Correlation Clustering
6955.content:
Online correlation clustering groups evolving time series according to the strength and consistency of their recent relationships. It updates compact statistics or assignments as new observations arrive instead of recomputing every pair over the complete history.

A sliding window or fading mechanism determines which past behavior remains relevant. The method must separate meaningful collective change from transient noise and adapt when formerly correlated series diverge.

6956.sourceSearchName: online correlation clustering online correlation clustering
6956.title: Online Correlation Clustering
6956.heading: References

6958.sourceSearchName: online analytical processing online analytical processing
6958.title: Online Analytical Processing
6958.heading: Online Analytical Processing
6958.content:
Online analytical processing provides interactive operations over multidimensional data, including paging, pivoting, sorting, filtering, drill-down, and drill-up. It supports fast exploration of aggregated organizational information.

OLAP can reveal candidate trends or segments through direct manipulation. Data mining extends that exploration with algorithms that infer patterns or models not specified as a sequence of manual queries.

6959.sourceSearchName: online analytical processing online analytical processing
6959.title: Online Analytical Processing
6959.heading: References

6961.title: Online Algorithm
6961.heading: Online Algorithm
6961.content:
An online algorithm processes input incrementally rather than requiring the complete problem instance before it begins. At every point it maintains a solution based on the information received so far.

This property is useful when data arrive as a stream or future input is unknown. [[Insertion Sort]] can maintain an ordered collection as new items arrive, while a greedy edge-coloring procedure can schedule matches even when contestants join after scheduling has begun.

6963.sourceSearchName: one way anova one way anova
6963.title: One-Way ANOVA
6963.heading: Document

6964.sourceSearchName: one way anova one way anova
6964.title: One-Way ANOVA
6964.heading: One-Way ANOVA
6964.content:
A one-way analysis of variance tests whether a continuous outcome has the same mean across levels of one explanatory variable. It partitions variability into between-group and within-group components and compares them with an F statistic.

The explanatory variable may be represented continuously or as a factor, but those specifications test different structures. A significant omnibus result shows that not all group means are equal; it does not by itself identify which groups differ.

6965.sourceSearchName: one way anova one way anova
6965.title: One-Way ANOVA
6965.heading: References

6966.sourceSearchName: one point and two point tracking one point and two point tracking
6966.title: One-Point and Two-Point Tracking
6966.heading: Document

6967.sourceSearchName: one point and two point tracking one point and two point tracking
6967.title: One-Point and Two-Point Tracking
6967.heading: One-Point and Two-Point Tracking
6967.content: One tracked feature supplies the changing position needed for a translation match. Two features also expose how their relative angle and spacing change, permitting rotation and apparent scale to be matched. This still describes a planar image transform, not a full camera reconstruction. The book's tracking examples show why the number and arrangement of points should be chosen according to the movement the replacement element must follow. A surface that changes perspective may need [[Four-Point Corner Pin Tracking]].

6968.sourceSearchName: one point and two point tracking one point and two point tracking
6968.title: One-Point and Two-Point Tracking
6968.heading: References

6969.sourceSearchName: one versus rest classification one versus rest classification
6969.title: One-Versus-Rest Classification
6969.heading: Document

6970.sourceSearchName: one versus rest classification one versus rest classification
6970.title: One-Versus-Rest Classification
6970.heading: One-Versus-Rest Classification
6970.content:
One-versus-rest classification reduces a multiclass task to one binary model per class. Each model separates its designated class from the union of all remaining classes.

Prediction compares the models' scores and chooses the strongest response. Training only as many models as there are classes is efficient, but the negative groups are heterogeneous and raw scores from independently fitted classifiers may not be directly comparable.

6971.sourceSearchName: one versus rest classification one versus rest classification
6971.title: One-Versus-Rest Classification
6971.heading: References

6972.sourceSearchName: one versus one classification one versus one classification
6972.title: One-Versus-One Classification
6972.heading: Document

6973.sourceSearchName: one versus one classification one versus one classification
6973.title: One-Versus-One Classification
6973.heading: One-Versus-One Classification
6973.content:
One-versus-one classification trains a binary classifier for every pair of classes. Each model sees only the observations belonging to its two designated classes.

At prediction time, pairwise decisions are combined by voting or a coupling procedure. The individual problems may be simpler than one-versus-rest contrasts, but the number of models grows quadratically with the number of classes and their outputs can conflict.

6974.sourceSearchName: one versus one classification one versus one classification
6974.title: One-Versus-One Classification
6974.heading: References

6975.sourceSearchName: one sided limit one sided limit
6975.title: One-Sided Limit
6975.heading: Document

6976.sourceSearchName: one sided limit one sided limit
6976.title: One-Sided Limit
6976.heading: One-Sided Limit
6976.content: A one-sided limit considers inputs approaching a point from only one direction. The left-hand limit uses $x<a$, and the right-hand limit uses $x>a$. A two-sided [[Limit of a Function]] exists only when both one-sided limits exist and are equal, making the distinction essential at jumps, endpoints, and piecewise boundaries.

6977.sourceSearchName: one sided limit one sided limit
6977.title: One-Sided Limit
6977.heading: References

6978.sourceSearchName: one question design test one question design test
6978.title: One-Question Design Test
6978.heading: Document

6979.sourceSearchName: one question design test one question design test
6979.title: One-Question Design Test
6979.heading: One-Question Design Test
6979.content:
A one-question design test turns the game's central vision into a single criterion for evaluating proposed features and changes. Each element is judged by whether it strengthens the intended player experience.

The question helps maintain coherence when many appealing ideas compete for attention. It links daily decisions to the [[Game Concept]] and provides a compact defense against [[Scope Creep]].

6980.sourceSearchName: one question design test one question design test
6980.title: One-Question Design Test
6980.heading: References

6981.sourceSearchName: one dimensional heat conduction one dimensional heat conduction
6981.title: One-Dimensional Heat Conduction
6981.heading: Document

6982.sourceSearchName: one dimensional heat conduction one dimensional heat conduction
6982.title: One-Dimensional Heat Conduction
6982.heading: One-Dimensional Heat Conduction
6982.content:
One-dimensional heat conduction assumes temperature varies primarily along one coordinate. Line elements can represent layered walls or slender regions using conductivity, area, length, sources, and endpoint boundary conditions.

A composite wall is assembled from elements with different conductivities and thicknesses. Continuity at shared nodes produces a common interface temperature and conserved heat-flow rate.

6983.sourceSearchName: one dimensional heat conduction one dimensional heat conduction
6983.title: One-Dimensional Heat Conduction
6983.heading: References

6984.sourceSearchName: one hot encoding one hot encoding
6984.title: One-Hot Encoding
6984.heading: Document

6985.sourceSearchName: one hot encoding one hot encoding
6985.title: One-Hot Encoding
6985.heading: One-Hot Encoding
6985.content:
One-hot encoding converts a categorical feature into a collection of binary indicators, one for each category. Exactly one indicator is active for an ordinary single-valued category, so the representation preserves identity without imposing an artificial numerical order.

The method increases dimensionality, especially for high-cardinality features. It is appropriate when an algorithm needs numerical vectors, but the expanded representation may require sparse storage or feature selection.

6986.sourceSearchName: one hot encoding one hot encoding
6986.title: One-Hot Encoding
6986.heading: References

6987.sourceSearchName: on demand self service on demand self service
6987.title: On-Demand Self-Service
6987.heading: Document

6988.sourceSearchName: on demand self service on demand self service
6988.title: On-Demand Self-Service
6988.heading: On-Demand Self-Service
6988.content:
On-demand self-service lets a cloud consumer obtain or release computing capability when it is needed without waiting for routine manual interaction with the provider. A portal or automated interface can turn a request into provisioned resources almost immediately.

This characteristic requires more than spare virtual machines. Standardized offerings, orchestration, capacity management, reporting, and access controls must work together so that self-service remains dependable and governed.

6989.title: On-Demand Self-Service

6990.sourceSearchName: omega navigation system omega navigation system
6990.title: Omega Navigation System
6990.heading: Document

6991.sourceSearchName: omega navigation system omega navigation system
6991.title: Omega Navigation System
6991.heading: Omega Navigation System
6991.content: Omega was a global, passive radio-navigation system built around eight synchronized very-low-frequency transmitters. Its long wavelengths propagated through the Earth-ionosphere waveguide, allowing continuous worldwide coverage with relatively few stations. A receiver compared signals to obtain a two-dimensional position, but accuracy was only about two kilometers and the remote, high-power transmitter network was expensive to maintain. Omega demonstrated global coverage while also exposing the limits of terrestrial infrastructure.

6992.title: Omega Navigation System

6994.sourceSearchName: oltp and olap workloads oltp and olap workloads
6994.title: OLTP and OLAP Workloads
6994.heading: OLTP and OLAP Workloads
6994.content:
Online transaction processing records operational events such as orders, payments, and customer contacts. Online analytical processing asks historical, aggregated questions across those events, often by region, product, or time period. The two workloads therefore organize data for different purposes.

A warehouse and data cube can make predefined summaries quick to slice, pivot, and report. Those fixed dimensions also limit the questions the cube can express. OLAP supports exploration and reporting, but it does not itself learn a predictive model or discover every pattern the organization may need.

The design-patterns source contrasts an operational database optimized for frequent insert, update, and delete statements with an analytical store optimized for selections and aggregation. Indexes and other table structures accelerate reads but add maintenance cost to each write. A separate read store can protect transactional throughput while serving reporting needs, though it must be kept in sync with its source.

6995.sourceSearchName: oltp and olap workloads oltp and olap workloads
6995.title: OLTP and OLAP Workloads
6995.heading: References

6997.title: Offsite Backup
6997.heading: Offsite Backup
6997.content:
An offsite backup stores a recovery copy in a location separated from the primary system. A fire, theft, electrical event, or local configuration error can then damage the original environment without necessarily destroying its backup.

A cloud backup service can supply this geographic separation. Sensitive data should be protected before or during transfer, and the restoration path must remain available when the primary site is not.

7000.title: Offline Loading
7000.heading: Offline Loading
7000.content:
Offline loading allows a web application to start with selected resources when the device cannot reach the network. A service worker serves cached application files or a deliberate offline page instead of leaving startup entirely dependent on a live server.

This does not mean every feature remains available. Operations requiring fresh API or database data must expose their unavailable state and recover when connectivity returns.

7002.title: Observable
7002.heading: Document
7002.content:
2026-09-06 20:31

Status: #baby

Tags: [[HTTP API Integration]] [[Reactive Programming in .NET]]

7003.title: Observable
7003.heading: Observable
7003.content:
An observable represents a sequence of values or events that a consumer can subscribe to over time. It fits asynchronous client behavior because the producer can emit a result, an error, or later updates without blocking the caller.

Angular [[Angular HttpClient|HttpClient]] returns observables for HTTP operations. Components and services can transform, retry, or react to those streams, and an activity log can observe form changes without repeatedly polling the form model.

.NET's `IObservable<T>` expresses the producer side of the same general idea: an observer subscribes, receives notifications as values change, and can dispose of the subscription. The inventory example makes a product recorder the provider for several reporting observers, keeping the provider independent of each report's behavior.

7006.title: Odds Ratio
7006.heading: Odds Ratio
7006.content:
An odds ratio compares the odds of a binary outcome between a focal predictor state and its reference. It equals the exponential of a logistic regression coefficient when the predictor changes by one unit.

An odds ratio of one indicates equal odds, values above one indicate higher odds, and values below one indicate lower odds. Odds are not probabilities or risk ratios, so the distinction becomes important when the outcome is common.

7008.sourceSearchName: odds ratio confidence interval odds ratio confidence interval
7008.title: Odds Ratio Confidence Interval
7008.heading: Document

7009.sourceSearchName: odds ratio confidence interval odds ratio confidence interval
7009.title: Odds Ratio Confidence Interval
7009.heading: Odds Ratio Confidence Interval
7009.content:
An odds ratio confidence interval exponentiates the lower and upper confidence limits of a logistic coefficient. It communicates both the plausible magnitude of the association and the precision of the estimate on the odds-ratio scale.

An interval that includes one does not support a nonzero association at the corresponding two-sided level. Reporting the interval is generally more informative than reporting only a p-value because it shows which effect sizes remain compatible with the model.

7010.sourceSearchName: odds ratio confidence interval odds ratio confidence interval
7010.title: Odds Ratio Confidence Interval
7010.heading: References

7012.title: Ocularity
7012.heading: Ocularity
7012.content:
Ocularity describes how display imagery is delivered to the eyes. A monocular display serves one eye, a bi-ocular display presents the same image to both eyes, and a binocular display supplies a separately rendered view to each eye.

Only the binocular arrangement can reproduce stereoscopic disparity as a depth cue. The choice also affects hardware complexity, field coverage, comfort, and how consistently virtual content can be aligned with the physical view.

7015.title: Occlusion Refinement
7015.heading: Occlusion Refinement
7015.content:
Occlusion refinement improves the boundary where a coarse real-scene model decides visibility. The projected model supplies an initial contour, and evidence from the current camera image adjusts that contour toward the observed physical edge.

This lets a practical model support convincing masking without reproducing every surface detail. Refinement must remain temporally stable, since a boundary that changes unpredictably from frame to frame creates visible flicker.

7018.title: Occlusion Handling
7018.heading: Occlusion Handling
7018.content:
Occlusion handling determines which real or virtual surface should be visible at each image location. A real object in front of a virtual object must hide it, while a virtual object nearer to the viewpoint must cover the corresponding real pixels.

Correct depth ordering requires geometry or image-derived evidence about the physical scene. Missing or inaccurate boundaries create conspicuous cutouts because occlusion is a strong depth cue.

7021.title: Observer Pattern
7021.heading: Observer Pattern
7021.content: The observer pattern lets a subject notify registered observers when its state changes, without knowing the observers' concrete types. The book's C# subject raises an event after inventory quantity changes, and several observer objects subscribe through matching delegates. The subject remains loosely coupled to its consumers; subscription and unsubscription define who receives each update.

7024.title: Observation Model
7024.heading: Observation Model
7024.content:
An observation model gives the probability of a measurement conditioned on a hidden state. It expresses how an inaccessible state is expected to appear through an imperfect sensor or other evidence source.

During filtering, this likelihood reweights the predicted state distribution. An informative observation concentrates belief on states that could plausibly have produced the measured value.

7026.sourceSearchName: observation and outcome periods observation and outcome periods
7026.title: Observation and Outcome Periods
7026.heading: Document

7027.sourceSearchName: observation and outcome periods observation and outcome periods
7027.title: Observation and Outcome Periods
7027.heading: Observation and Outcome Periods
7027.content:
In a propensity model, the observation period supplies the input attributes, while a later outcome period determines whether the predicted event occurred. The interval between them defines how far ahead the prediction is meant to work.

For churn, a model intended to warn two months before departure must train on information that would have been available two months before each historic customer's departure. Using later activity in the inputs would create a misleadingly easy task and leave too little time for an actual retention intervention.

7030.heading: Observable Mobile Repository
7030.content:
An observable mobile repository exposes a stream of data results rather than returning only one final collection. It can publish a cached local result immediately and later publish a refreshed remote result, allowing the view model to react without coordinating both stores directly.

This arrangement separates storage selection from presentation logic. Subscribers still need clear rules for ordering, completion, errors, and whether a later result replaces or merges with the earlier value.

7033.title: Oblique Mercator Route Alignment
7033.heading: Oblique Mercator Route Alignment
7033.content: An oblique Mercator reorients the cylinder so the line of tangency follows a selected great-circle corridor rather than the Equator or a meridian. Distortion is minimized along that oblique reference, allowing a long route to be represented inside the chart's useful band. The method is a projection equivalent of rotating coordinates to fit the path of interest.

7036.title: Objective Probability
7036.heading: Objective Probability
7036.content:
Objective probability interprets probability as a property or model of the external phenomenon rather than as a representation of a reasoner's knowledge. Under this view, randomness or noise is attributed to the world being modeled.

The book contrasts this with subjective probability, which makes preliminary knowledge explicit. The interpretive choice changes how uncertainty, unknown information, and model error are explained even when the same probability calculations are used.

For data science, an objective, nonfrequency account can ground probability in symmetries of a phenomenon's causal structure. When a [[Causal Symmetry]] leaves the determining conditions unchanged under relabeling, the symmetric outcomes receive equal probability.

7039.title: Objective Function
7039.heading: Objective Function
7039.content:
An objective function assigns a value to each candidate solution in an optimization problem. The task is to find a permitted point that minimizes or maximizes this value.

In [[Linear Programming]], the objective is linear. In [[Nonlinear Programming]], either the objective or at least one constraint is nonlinear. The objective must be interpreted together with the [[Feasible Solution|feasible solutions]] defined by the constraints.

7041.title: Object-Relational Mapping

7042.sourceSearchName: object relational mapping object relational mapping
7042.title: Object-Relational Mapping
7042.heading: Object-Relational Mapping
7042.content:
Object-relational mapping connects an object-oriented application model to tables, columns, keys, and relationships in a relational database. It allows code to create, read, update, and delete persistent data through typed objects instead of writing every data-access operation directly.

[[Entity Framework Core]] performs this mapping from entity classes and a [[Database Context]]. Conventions and [[Data Annotation|annotations]] define how class members correspond to the database model.

7043.sourceSearchName: object relational mapping object relational mapping
7043.title: Object-Relational Mapping
7043.heading: References

7044.sourceSearchName: object oriented middleware object oriented middleware
7044.title: Object-Oriented Middleware
7044.heading: Document

7045.sourceSearchName: object oriented middleware object oriented middleware
7045.title: Object-Oriented Middleware
7045.heading: Object-Oriented Middleware
7045.content:
Object-oriented middleware allows one application to invoke or reuse code represented as an object supplied by another application or service. The integration boundary is a callable behavior and its interface rather than a shared database or queued message.

This can provide direct reuse but can also couple participants to interface, execution, and failure assumptions. The book distinguishes it from [[Message-Oriented Middleware]] and [[Data-Oriented Middleware]] as a separate integration style.

7046.sourceSearchName: object oriented middleware object oriented middleware
7046.title: Object-Oriented Middleware
7046.heading: References

7048.title: Object Selection
7048.heading: Object Selection
7048.content:
Object selection is the task of acquiring or identifying one object or a subset of objects from the available set. It is also called target acquisition and is a canonical [[3D Manipulation]] task.

Selection difficulty depends on target size and distance, object density, occlusion, number of targets, input precision, and the [[Depth Cue]]s provided by the display. Pointing techniques often perform well for remote selection, while grasping techniques are generally more suitable for subsequent manipulation.

Dense scenes can use [[Progressive Refinement]]: a coarse first action narrows the candidates and a simpler second action identifies the final target.

7051.title: Object Rotation
7051.heading: Object Rotation
7051.content:
Object rotation changes an object's orientation. It is a canonical [[3D Manipulation]] task whose difficulty depends on the initial and target orientations, the amount of rotation, distance to the object, and required precision.

An [[Input Device]] that integrates rotational degrees of freedom can support coordinated movement, but its grip and range matter. A precision grip can use smaller finger muscles for fine rotation, while a limited hand or device range may force [[Clutching]].

Directionally compliant [[Feedback]] makes the virtual object rotate in the same direction as the physical control, helping the user predict the result.

7054.title: Object Scaling
7054.heading: Object Scaling
7054.content:
Object scaling changes the size of an object. Unlike selection, positioning, and rotation, it has no direct everyday counterpart, but it is a common manipulation in two- and three-dimensional interfaces.

Scaling tasks vary by initial size, target size, amount of change, distance to the object, and required precision. A technique should make the scale factor and reference point clear through its mapping and [[Feedback]].

Object scaling is a canonical [[3D Manipulation]] task and should remain distinct from scaling an entire world for [[3D Travel]] or viewpoint control.

7057.title: Object Positioning
7057.heading: Object Positioning
7057.content:
Object positioning changes the three-dimensional location of an object. It is one of the canonical tasks of [[3D Manipulation]].

The task can vary by the distance and direction to the initial and target positions, the total translation distance, and the precision required. A direct spatial mapping may make coarse movement intuitive, but large control-display gain can amplify hand jitter and make precise placement difficult.

Constraints can remove unnecessary [[Degrees of Freedom]], while suitable [[Feedback]] helps the user judge when the object has reached the intended location.

7060.title: Object Picking
7060.heading: Object Picking
7060.content:
Object picking determines which world object corresponds to a screen position selected by the player. The screen point is [[Unprojection|unprojected]] at near and far depths to construct a world-space ray.

The program intersects that ray with candidate collision geometry and chooses the nearest valid hit. The accuracy and cost of picking depend on whether the test uses coarse bounds, detailed geometry, or a staged combination.

7063.title: Object Layering
7063.heading: Object Layering
7063.content:
Object layering combines game objects whose behaviors create a stronger situation together than either creates alone. Different movement patterns, threats, or reactions can require the player to track and manage several relationships at once.

Layering works best after each object has received a clear [[Rule Introduction]]. Without that prior understanding, the combination becomes a trap based on hidden information rather than a [[Meaningful Decision|meaningful choice]].

7066.title: OAuth Resource
7066.heading: OAuth Resource
7066.content:
An OAuth resource is the protected service for which an access token is intended. The stock-checker API is registered as a resource, and its authentication middleware treats the IdentityServer authority as the issuer whose tokens it will validate.

A token meant for one resource should not be treated as general permission across every service. Resource configuration gives the authorization server and API a shared name for the boundary being protected.

7069.title: OAuth Scope
7069.heading: OAuth Scope
7069.content:
An OAuth scope names a permission or access boundary a client may request for a resource. Scopes help limit a token to the part of a service the client actually needs rather than granting undifferentiated authority.

The book's IdentityServer configuration associates its client with the protected API scope before requesting a token. Application-specific role checks can further narrow individual operations after the token has established access to the resource.

7071.sourceSearchName: oauth grant type oauth grant type
7071.title: OAuth Grant Type
7071.heading: Document

7072.sourceSearchName: oauth grant type oauth grant type
7072.title: OAuth Grant Type
7072.heading: OAuth Grant Type
7072.content:
An OAuth grant type defines the interaction through which a client obtains authorization and an access token. It identifies which participant supplies credentials, what trust the client receives, and whether user interaction occurs at the authorization server.

Grant selection is a security and usability decision rather than a interchangeable configuration label. The book examines the limitations of its [[Resource Owner Password Grant]] and notes that a server-hosted login can keep sensitive authentication logic out of desktop code.

7073.sourceSearchName: oauth grant type oauth grant type
7073.title: OAuth Grant Type
7073.heading: References

7075.title: OAuth Client
7075.heading: OAuth Client
7075.content:
An OAuth client is the application requesting an access token so it can call a protected resource. IdentityServer configuration identifies the client, its allowed grant, credentials, and the scopes or API resources it may request.

In the stock checker, the UWP application is the client and the ASP.NET Core API is the resource. Defining the client in the authorization server makes its permitted path to a token an explicit part of the system's trust model.

7078.title: OAuth 2.0
7078.heading: OAuth 2.0
7078.content:
OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework in which a client obtains an access token for a protected resource instead of sending a user's credentials with every API request. The participants and grant define how that token is requested and what it can be used to access.

The stock-checker project uses IdentityServer 4 to issue a token to a UWP client and configures an ASP.NET Core API to validate it. Authentication establishes the user, while role-sensitive authorization still decides whether that user may read or update stock.

7081.title: Numerical Prediction
7081.heading: Numerical Prediction
7081.content:
Numerical prediction estimates a quantitative outcome such as visits, votes, revenue, or an influence score. Unlike ranking or classification, the distance between predicted and observed values is meaningful.

Correlation-based evaluation measures whether both values move together, while error-based evaluation measures their direct disagreement. A model can correlate strongly yet still be systematically miscalibrated, so the two views answer different questions.

7083.title: Numerical Representation for Computation
7083.heading: Document

7084.sourceSearchName: numerical representation for computation numerical representation for computation
7084.title: Numerical Representation for Computation
7084.heading: Numerical Representation for Computation
7084.content:
Computation begins by representing quantities or phenomena with numbers, equations, symbols, or models in an agreed form. The representation determines which operations become possible and which features of the original situation are retained or omitted.

Digital computation extends this practice by encoding information into machine-processable data. A useful representation therefore connects meaning in the domain to transformations the selected machine can reliably perform.

7085.title: Numerical Representation for Computation
7085.heading: References

7087.title: Numerical Inference
7087.heading: Numerical Inference
7087.content:
Numerical inference evaluates a probabilistic question using concrete sums, integrals, optimizations, or samples. It is required when symbolic simplification does not produce a usable analytic form.

The method chosen depends on whether variables are discrete or continuous, the dimension of the free-variable space, and whether the goal is a complete distribution, an expectation, or a most probable assignment.

7090.title: Numerical Feature
7090.heading: Numerical Feature
7090.content:
A numerical feature takes quantitative values for which ordering and differences can carry meaning. Examples include age, length, count, or a continuous sensor measurement.

Numerical domains support comparisons and notions of nearness that many analytic methods use directly. Their scale still matters: a ratio-scaled feature permits meaningful multiplicative statements, while other numerical measurements may support differences without making ratios meaningful.

7093.title: Numerical Coefficient
7093.heading: Numerical Coefficient
7093.content:
A numerical coefficient is the numerical factor multiplying the variable part of an [[Algebraic Term]]. In (13a^2b^3), the coefficient is (13); in (-ac), the unwritten coefficient is (-1).

Coefficients describe how many copies of the same variable structure occur. The [[Distributive Property]] therefore permits coefficients of [[Like Terms]] to be added: (5x-2x=(5-2)x=3x). A missing written coefficient of a positive term is one, not zero.

7095.sourceSearchName: number of clusters problem number of clusters problem
7095.title: Number of Clusters Problem
7095.heading: Document

7096.sourceSearchName: number of clusters problem number of clusters problem
7096.title: Number of Clusters Problem
7096.heading: Number of Clusters Problem
7096.content:
The number of clusters problem asks how many groups provide the most useful representation of a data set. A hierarchical tree supports many cut levels, while a partition method such as K-means generally requires a value of k before fitting.

There may be several defensible answers at different resolutions. Objective functions, validity indices, stability tests, visualizations, and domain knowledge provide evidence, but none makes cluster count independent of purpose.

7097.sourceSearchName: number of clusters problem number of clusters problem
7097.title: Number of Clusters Problem
7097.heading: References

7099.title: Numerator
7099.heading: Numerator
7099.content:
The numerator is the upper component (m) of a [[Fraction]] (m/n). It records how many of the equal parts determined by the denominator are being taken and serves as the dividend in the equivalent division (m\div n).

A numerator may be larger than the [[Denominator]], producing an [[Improper Fraction]]. In fraction multiplication, numerators multiply with numerators. In addition or subtraction, numerators can be combined directly only after the fractions have been expressed with a [[Common Denominator]].

7102.title: Number Line
7102.heading: Number Line
7102.content:
A number line represents ordered numbers as points on a straight line. Values increase to the right and decrease to the left, with zero separating positive and negative directions.

The representation gives geometric meaning to several algebraic ideas. Addition can be understood as directed movement, an [[Opposite Number]] as reflection across zero, and [[Absolute Value]] as distance from zero. Inequality solutions can be graphed as rays or segments, with filled and open endpoints recording whether boundary values belong to the solution set.

7105.title: NUMA Affinity
7105.heading: NUMA Affinity
7105.content:
NUMA affinity places a thread and the memory or device queues it frequently accesses on the same non-uniform memory access node. Local placement avoids cross-socket transfers with higher latency and shared interconnect cost.

For a high-rate storage path, interrupt handling, buffers, worker threads, and network interfaces should be assigned with the machine's memory topology in mind.

7108.content:
A value type normally always contains a value, but appending `?` creates a nullable form that can also represent `null`. This is useful when a number, date, or other value is absent in an external source such as a database.

A nullable value reports whether it has a value and exposes that value only when present. Code should test or safely unwrap it before use. The null-coalescing operator can provide a fallback when absence has a sensible default.

7111.sourceSearchName: nullable reference types nullable reference types
7111.title: Nullable Reference Types
7111.heading: Nullable Reference Types
7111.content:
C# 8.0 introduced an opt-in analysis mode that distinguishes reference variables intended to allow `null` from those expected to remain non-null. A `?` marks a nullable reference, while an unmarked reference produces compiler warnings when code may assign or dereference null unsafely.

This feature changes static analysis rather than the underlying runtime representation. It documents intent and moves many possible null-reference failures into compiler feedback, but callers and implementations must still check data that can genuinely be absent.

The desktop migration chapter shows the C# 8 feature as opt-in analysis that can be enabled for a file with `#nullable enable` or for a whole project in its project file. It uses constructor initialization and nullable annotations to distinguish values that must exist from those allowed to be absent.

7114.sourceSearchName: null proportion estimate null proportion estimate
7114.title: Null Proportion Estimate
7114.heading: Null Proportion Estimate
7114.content:
A null proportion estimate approximates the fraction of tested features whose [[Null Hypothesis|null hypotheses]] are true. The source estimates it from the share of p-values above a relatively high threshold, where most observations are assumed to come from true nulls.

Using this information can make false-discovery estimates less conservative than assuming every null is true. The estimate depends on threshold choice and on the expected p-value behavior under the null.

7117.title: Null Hypothesis
7117.heading: Null Hypothesis
7117.content:
A null hypothesis specifies the skeptical scenario against which an observed result is compared, commonly that a treatment produces no population difference. It is a model of what the data-generating process would look like without the effect being investigated.

Evidence is evaluated through the [[Null Distribution]] of a chosen statistic. Failing to reject the null does not prove it true; it means the observation was not sufficiently inconsistent with that model under the test's assumptions.

7120.title: Null Distribution
7120.heading: Null Distribution
7120.content:
A null distribution is the probability distribution of a test statistic when the [[Null Hypothesis]] is true. It describes the variation expected from sampling or random assignment without the effect under investigation.

The position of the observed statistic within this distribution determines a [[P-Value]]. The distribution may come from mathematical theory, a [[Parametric Simulation]], or a [[Permutation Test]], depending on the design and available assumptions.

7126.title: Nuclear Fusion
7126.heading: Nuclear Fusion
7126.content: Nuclear fusion joins light nuclei into heavier products and releases energy when the product mass is lower than the reactants' mass. The source relates the difference to $\Delta E=\Delta mc^2$. Useful terrestrial power requires nuclei energetic enough to overcome repulsion, a hot confined plasma with enough reactions, and equipment to capture the released heat. This is distinct from splitting heavy nuclei in fission.

7129.title: Nuclear Fission
7129.heading: Nuclear Fission
7129.content: Nuclear fission splits a heavy nucleus into two medium-mass fragments, neutrons, and released energy. Neutrons from one event can trigger further fissions, producing a chain reaction. A reactor controls neutron population and removes heat, while an uncontrolled supercritical assembly releases energy rapidly.

7132.title: NSFNET
7132.heading: NSFNET
7132.content:
NSFNET was a National Science Foundation network created to connect researchers with supercomputer centers and one another. It adopted TCP/IP and welcomed general academic traffic rather than serving only one discipline.

Regional networks connected to its national backbone, allowing the system to expand beyond ARPANET. NSFNET became the principal bridge from a government research network to the broadly accessible Internet.

7134.sourceSearchName: nuclear binding energy nuclear binding energy

7134.heading: Document

7135.sourceSearchName: nuclear binding energy nuclear binding energy
7135.title: Nuclear Binding Energy
7135.heading: Nuclear Binding Energy
7135.content: Nuclear binding energy is the work required to separate a nucleus into free protons and neutrons. The bound nucleus has less mass than those separated nucleons; the mass defect corresponds to energy through $E=mc^2$. Binding energy per nucleon compares stability and explains energy release from both fission of heavy nuclei and fusion of light nuclei.

7138.sourceSearchName: nuclear fission power plant nuclear fission power plant
7138.title: Nuclear Fission Power Plant
7138.heading: Nuclear Fission Power Plant
7138.content: A fission power plant uses reactor heat to raise steam, then passes that steam through a turbine-generator much like a [[Steam Power Plant]]. The source's comparison concerns the conversion arrangement: nuclear reaction replaces fuel combustion as the heat source, but thermal, mechanical, and electrical stages remain. This differs from the separate proposed [[Nuclear Fusion]] heat source discussed later in the book.

7141.title: NSFNET Backbone
7141.heading: NSFNET Backbone
7141.content:
The NSFNET backbone connected regional and institutional networks through high-speed national links. It advanced from T1 service at roughly 1.5 megabits per second to T3 service at roughly 45 megabits per second.

Contractors such as MCI built and operated the links. The backbone architecture encouraged private providers to create networks that could eventually assume commercial Internet traffic.

7144.sourceSearchName: novelty preference in games novelty preference in games
7144.title: Novelty Preference in Games
7144.heading: Novelty Preference in Games
7144.content:
Novelty preference is the desire for variety, surprise, unfamiliar settings, and new rules or experiences. It is associated with openness to experience in the source's player-motivation model.

Players low in novelty seeking may prefer familiar structures and dependable repetition. A design can signal how much learning and uncertainty it expects rather than assuming every player values constant change.

7147.title: NoSQL Database
7147.heading: NoSQL Database
7147.content:
A NoSQL database uses a data model other than the traditional relational table-and-join model. The category includes document, key-value, graph, and other stores whose structures and scaling choices fit different access patterns.

Cosmos DB supplies a [[Document Database]] in the project, while its API compatibility lets the application use MongoDB conventions. Choosing NoSQL is therefore not merely choosing the cloud; it is choosing storage and query semantics that should match the application's data relationships.

7150.title: Normalized Spectral Clustering
7150.heading: Normalized Spectral Clustering
7150.content:
Normalized spectral clustering rescales the graph Laplacian by vertex degrees before extracting its eigenvectors. The normalization relates graph separation to the volume of a region rather than only the raw number or weight of cut edges.

This discourages trivial cuts that isolate a few low-degree vertices and often handles unequal graph density better. Very small degrees and disconnected components still require care during normalization and interpretation.

Normative judgmental analysis directs judges to rank each profile using the supplied predictor variables. The common attribute set provides the basis for estimating and comparing decision equations.

Restricting attention to the predictors makes differences among policies easier to interpret. It also means that omitted factors cannot be recovered from the fitted equation.

7159.title: Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain
7159.heading: Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain
7159.content:
Normalized discounted cumulative gain evaluates a ranked list by rewarding relevant items more when they occur near the top. Logarithmic discount reduces the contribution of relevance found at lower positions.

Dividing the observed discounted gain by the ideal ordering yields a value between zero and one. This normalization permits rankings with different relevance scales to be compared at selected cutoff positions.

7162.sourceSearchName: normalized floating point number normalized floating point number
7162.title: Normalized Floating-Point Number
7162.heading: Normalized Floating-Point Number
7162.content:
A normalized floating-point number places its first nonzero digit at a fixed position in the mantissa. This removes redundant representations and uses the available digits efficiently.

The allowed mantissa length limits precision, while the exponent range limits magnitude. Values outside the range overflow or underflow, and values between representable numbers require [[Rounding]] or [[Chopping]].

7165.heading: Normalized Device Coordinates
7165.content:
Normalized device coordinates are the standardized coordinates used after vertex projection and perspective division. In OpenGL, visible horizontal and vertical positions generally span from minus one to one, with depth represented in the API's normalized range.

The viewport maps this normalized cube to screen pixels. A basic 2D program can author vertices directly in this space, while a 3D program reaches it through world, view, and projection transformations.

7168.title: Normalized Cut Relaxation
7168.heading: Normalized Cut Relaxation
7168.content:
Normalized cut evaluates each group's boundary relative to the total edge weight incident on that group. It therefore balances separation against graph volume and is sensitive to connectivity rather than group size alone.

Its discrete optimization is relaxed to a generalized or normalized Laplacian eigenproblem. The final partition remains an approximation whose quality depends on how continuous eigenvectors are discretized.
